beats.intro: Chapter five. [[sub]]How governments steer an economy: through money and interest rates, and through taxing and spending.
beats.policy: [[a]]Governments steer the economy with two kinds of policy. [[mon]]Monetary policy is run by the central bank. It influences the quantity of money and credit, and so interest rates. [[fis]]Fiscal policy is run by the government. It decides taxation and spending. [[goal]]Both aim for the same thing: stable growth and low, stable inflation. They can speed up a slowing economy, or cool an overheating one.
beats.money: [[a]]To see how policy works, start with money. Money does three jobs. [[m1]]It is a medium of exchange: you can pay with it. [[m2]]It is a unit of account: prices are quoted in it. [[m3]]And it is a store of value: it carries purchasing power into the future. [[def]]Narrow money is notes, coins and current-account deposits. Broad money adds less liquid deposits as well.
beats.create: [[a]]Banks create money by lending. Suppose banks keep ten percent of deposits in reserve. [[b1]]You deposit one hundred euros. The bank keeps ten, and lends ninety. [[b2]]The borrower spends it, and the seller deposits ninety in a second bank. That bank keeps nine, and lends eighty-one. [[b3]]The third bank keeps eight point one, and lends seventy-two point nine. [[more]]And so on, round after round. [[tot]]All the deposits add up to the original deposit, divided by the reserve requirement: one hundred over point one, or one thousand. [[mult]]The money multiplier is one divided by the reserve requirement: ten. The lower the reserve requirement, the bigger the multiplier.
beats.qty: [[a]]The quantity equation links money to prices: M times V equals P times Y. [[m]]M is the money supply. V is velocity, how often each unit changes hands. P is the price level, and Y is real output. [[ex]]Suppose velocity and output stay fixed, and the money supply rises ten percent. [[p]]Then the price level must rise ten percent. This is money neutrality: in the long run, more money means higher prices, not more output.
beats.mdemand: [[a]]People hold money for three reasons: to make transactions, as a precaution, and for speculation. [[dem]]The interest rate is the cost of holding money instead of bonds, so money demand slopes down. [[sup]]The central bank sets the money supply: a vertical line. [[eq]]They meet at the equilibrium interest rate. [[shift]]Now the central bank expands the money supply. [[low]]With more money chasing the same demand, the interest rate falls.
beats.fisher: [[a]]The Fisher effect says: the nominal interest rate equals the real rate, plus expected inflation. [[ex]]Suppose the real rate is two percent, and expected inflation is three. The nominal rate is five. [[up]]Now expected inflation rises to six. [[nom]]The nominal rate rises to eight. The real rate has not moved. [[why]]That is the idea behind money neutrality: money growth changes inflation expectations, but not the real rate.
beats.costs: [[a]]Inflation has costs. But expected and unexpected inflation differ. [[exp]]Expected inflation can be built into wages, prices and contracts. Its costs are small: [[exp2]]you hold less cash, and firms change price lists more often. [[unexp]]Unexpected inflation is the costly kind. [[red]]If inflation is higher than expected, borrowers gain and lenders lose. If it is lower, lenders gain. [[unc]]Uncertain inflation also makes lenders demand a premium, raising borrowing costs and discouraging investment. [[sig]]And it blurs price signals: a firm may mistake general inflation for higher demand, expand, and then have to cut back.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Monetary policy works through money and rates; fiscal policy through taxes and spending. [[w2]]Banks create money by lending, with a multiplier of one over the reserve requirement. [[w3]]More money raises prices in the long run, and lowers the interest rate in the short run. [[w4]]The nominal rate is the real rate plus expected inflation, and unexpected inflation is the most costly.
